analysis.one_liner: Blocks brokers and advisers from steering non-accredited investors into high-fee SPACs without strict disclosures.
analysis.headline: The House Financial Services Committee advanced the bill on a 29-23 vote, but it never received a floor vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: A SPAC is a shell company that goes public and then merges with a private company, giving the private company's owners a shortcut to a stock listing. SPAC sponsors and the brokers who sell SPAC shares typically take large fees, and ordinary investors often bear those costs after the stock falls. This bill would prohibit investment advisers, brokers, and their representatives from recommending or selling SPAC securities to people who are not accredited investors unless the sponsor's economic compensation (the 'promote') is 5% or less, or the SPAC makes disclosures to the Securities and Exchange Commission that the SEC deems necessary to protect investors.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary investors who do not meet the accredited-investor test (generally higher incomes, net worth, or financial expertise). They would be shielded from being steered into SPAC deals where sponsors and intermediaries take large cuts that come out of shareholders' returns.

how_it_helps.text: The bill prohibits investment advisers, brokers, and their registered representatives from facilitating or recommending SPAC securities to non-accredited investors unless the sponsor's promote is 5% or less, or the SPAC makes SEC-determined investor-protection disclosures.
SPACs are shell companies that raise money in an IPO to acquire other companies; the CRS summary describes the bill's target as limiting recommendations of certain SPAC securities.
By conditioning the sales practice on either a low sponsor fee or mandated disclosures, the bill forces the fees that skim SPAC investors' returns into the open or off the table for small investors.

analysis.who_pays: SPAC sponsors, whose 'promote' typically runs far above 5% of the deal, plus the investment banks and brokers that earn fees selling SPAC shares to retail customers. They would either cut their fees or lose access to non-accredited investors.

drawbacks.text: The bill restricts what non-accredited investors may buy: a retail investor who wanted to back a specific SPAC deal could be barred from doing so, trading access for protection.

The disclosure pathway leaves the sales practice fully open as long as a SPAC files the required disclosures with the SEC, so a well-counseled sponsor could keep charging high fees and simply disclose them.
Compliance would fall on brokers and advisers to screen every SPAC recommendation by investor status, adding costs that the financial services industry would argue get passed to customers.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real: retail investors were being sold SPAC shares at the tail end of a boom in which sponsors and banks captured large fees and many SPAC stocks later fell, so limiting or forcing disclosure of those fees protects less-sophisticated investors. The cost is reduced choice for non-accredited investors, and the disclosure exception means sponsors who accept transparency can keep charging high fees. On balance the bill would shift money from intermediaries to small investors, though its reach is narrower than the title suggests because it applies only to recommended or broker-facilitated sales, not to purchases an investor makes on their own initiative.

outcome.mechanism: The committee voted the bill out 29-23, but no one ever scheduled a floor vote and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the bill on November 9, 2021, and it was referred to the House Committee on Financial Services.
On November 16, 2021, the committee held a markup and ordered the bill to be reported in the nature of a substitute (amended) by a recorded vote of 29-23.

After the committee vote, no further action appears in the record: the bill was never reported to the full House in the form available, never debated on the floor, and received no vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2023.
The bill drew no cosponsors in the House.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: SPAC sponsors and the banks and brokers that charge high fees selling SPAC shares are better off: the bill never became law, so the status quo in which retail investors can be sold SPAC securities regardless of sponsor compensation continues. House leadership is also spared a vote it never scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: The record shows only a 29-23 committee vote without a party breakdown; the close margin on a Democratic-led committee suggests the vote largely followed party lines, but the sources do not confirm how each side split.

industries.note: Sponsors typically take a 'promote' far above the bill's 5% threshold; the bill would cut their pay or lock retail investors out of deals where they keep it. Their fees come directly out of SPAC shareholders' returns.

Banks underwrite SPACs and brokers earn commissions selling SPAC shares to retail customers; the bill would bar or restrict those sales to non-accredited investors unless fees are cut or disclosures are filed.
Non-accredited investors would stop being steered into deals where sponsor fees skim their returns, though they would also lose the option to buy SPAC shares on a broker's recommendation.
